title: PostgreSQL Dialect Features and Portability
learningObjectives: Explain the purpose of RETURNING and ON CONFLICT.
Distinguish ILIKE from portable case-normalization patterns.
Identify PostgreSQL features that SQLite cannot execute directly.
Label PostgreSQL-only examples and verify them against the target version.

understand.concept: PostgreSQL provides a standards-oriented SQL implementation with additional features such as JSONB, arrays, RETURNING, ILIKE, rich type support and advanced indexing.
understand.whyItMatters: Using PostgreSQL features can simplify application code, but those features should be deliberately chosen and isolated when portability matters.
understand.analogy: A toolkit may include specialist tools that are excellent for one workshop but are not available in every workshop.
understand.analogyLimit: A PostgreSQL feature may have no direct SQLite equivalent, and similar-looking syntax can have different type, collation or transaction behaviour.

explain.narrative:
## PostgreSQL extensions and capabilities
PostgreSQL supports `RETURNING` on data-modification statements, `ILIKE` for case-insensitive pattern matching, `JSONB` for binary JSON storage, arrays, UUID types, identity columns and `DISTINCT ON` as a product-specific query feature.

## Conflict handling
PostgreSQL supports `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (...) DO UPDATE` with explicit conflict targets. SQLite also supports an UPSERT form, but supported clauses, constraints and edge-case behaviour must be checked against the relevant versions.

## Time and type semantics
PostgreSQL distinguishes timestamp with and without time zone and provides rich numeric, range and user-defined types. Do not replace TIMESTAMPTZ with arbitrary text without a deliberate time-zone model.

## Runnable examples
The examples below use SQLite-compatible relational SQL. PostgreSQL-only syntax is shown in the explanation as a labelled dialect reference and must be tested in PostgreSQL before use.

examples.title: Create a portable account table
examples.code: CREATE TABLE dialect23_accounts (account_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, email TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE, account_state TEXT NOT NULL);
examples.explanation: Creates a simple account relation. PostgreSQL would commonly use BIGINT or GENERATED AS IDENTITY for the key and may use CITEXT or a suitable unique expression for case-insensitive email policy.

examples.title: Insert sample accounts
examples.explanation: Adds two synthetic accounts. PostgreSQL can return inserted values directly with INSERT ... RETURNING; this SQLite-compatible example reads them in a separate statement.

examples.title: Read the inserted account rows
examples.code: SELECT account_id, email, account_state FROM dialect23_accounts ORDER BY account_id;
examples.explanation: Uses a portable SELECT projection. In PostgreSQL, `INSERT INTO ... VALUES (...) RETURNING account_id, email` can return generated or inserted values in the same statement.

examples.title: Use a portable case-normalized lookup
examples.code: SELECT account_id, email FROM dialect23_accounts WHERE lower(email) = lower('ASHA@example.test');
examples.explanation: Demonstrates a case-normalized comparison. PostgreSQL offers ILIKE for case-insensitive pattern matching; collation and index strategy still matter.

examples.title: Use a SQLite/PostgreSQL-compatible conflict update pattern
examples.code: INSERT INTO dialect23_accounts (account_id, email, account_state) VALUES (1, 'asha@example.test', 'active') ON CONFLICT(account_id) DO UPDATE SET account_state = excluded.account_state; SELECT account_id, account_state FROM dialect23_accounts WHERE account_id = 1;
examples.explanation: Uses an UPSERT form supported by modern SQLite and PostgreSQL. Conflict target rules and available RETURNING behaviour should be verified for the target engine version.

practise.guidedTask: Run the portable examples and identify where PostgreSQL offers a direct extension such as RETURNING or ILIKE. Explain why an extension must be tested separately from the SQLite lesson runtime.
practise.independentTask: Design a PostgreSQL-specific customer table using an identity key, TIMESTAMPTZ and JSONB metadata. Label each type and write a portable fallback or migration note for another DBMS.
hints: PostgreSQL supports RETURNING for data changes.
JSONB and arrays are PostgreSQL type features.
SQLite execution does not validate PostgreSQL-only syntax.

questions.prompt: Which PostgreSQL feature returns values from an INSERT or UPDATE statement?
questions.explanation: PostgreSQL supports RETURNING on data-modification statements.

questions.prompt: Which operator is PostgreSQL-specific for case-insensitive pattern matching?
questions.explanation: ILIKE performs case-insensitive pattern matching in PostgreSQL.
JSONB stores parsed JSON in a binary representation with indexing support.

questions.prompt: Why should TIMESTAMPTZ be chosen deliberately?
options: It represents time-zone-aware instants and has conversion semantics
It stores only a calendar date
It is the same as arbitrary text
questions.answer: It represents time-zone-aware instants and has conversion semantics
questions.explanation: Time-zone semantics affect storage and display of instants.

questions.prompt: Does a SQLite test prove a PostgreSQL-only ILIKE query works?
options: No; test it in the target PostgreSQL version
Only when the table is empty
questions.answer: No; test it in the target PostgreSQL version
questions.explanation: Dialect-specific syntax requires execution against that DBMS.
